theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Chapter 5 Formula & Fact Drill
Your quick-revision summary, checked and corrected:
items: OSI has 7 layers, remembered from layer 7 down as 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing': Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data link, Physical. The TCP/IP model has 4, remembered from the top as 'A T I N': Application, Transport, Internet, Network access.

Devices: a hub repeats every bit out of all its other ports (layer 1), a switch forwards each frame by destination MAC address (layer 2), and a router forwards each packet by destination IP address (layer 3).

TCP is connection-oriented and reliable, with sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmission, flow control and congestion control; UDP is connectionless best effort with an 8-byte header. 'Slow' and 'fast' describe TCP's extra set-up and recovery work, not the speed of the link.
Well-known ports: FTP 20/21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, HTTP 80, POP3 110, IMAP 143, HTTPS 443.
Classful IPv4 by first octet: A 1–126 (0 is reserved and 127 is loopback), B 128–191, C 192–223, D 224–239 for multicast, E 240–255 reserved.
Routing: RIP is distance vector (hop count, 15 at most), OSPF is link state (cost, Dijkstra, faster convergence), and BGP is the path vector protocol between autonomous systems such as ISPs.
Security rests on CIA: confidentiality, integrity and availability. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key (AES); asymmetric encryption uses a public/private key pair (RSA, ECC).
Wi-Fi security: WEP is broken and must never be used, WPA with TKIP is deprecated as well, WPA2 with AES-CCMP is the minimum and WPA3 is preferred.

theoryAdd.text: Your memory tricks and common traps, with the fine print added:
items: TCP = 'Tried and Checked Properly' (reliable); UDP = 'Unreliable but Damn fast Packets' (no handshake, no retransmission).
Port 80 = HTTP: H is the 8th letter of the alphabet. Port 443 = HTTPS: 'HTTPS Secure' has 11 letters, and 4 + 4 + 3 = 11.
ARP finds a MAC address from an IP address; RARP did the reverse and has been replaced by DHCP. DNS finds an IP address from a name.
SMTP sends and relays mail (port 25 between servers, 587 for submission from clients); POP3 (110) and IMAP (143) only retrieve it.
A hub repeats everything it receives out of all its other ports; a switch sends a frame only to the destination's port once it has learned that address, and floods it until then.
TCP opens with a 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), but a normal close takes 4 segments (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK), or 3 when one side combines its ACK and FIN.
If an option offers WEP beside WPA2 or WPA3, WEP is never the secure answer, whatever its key length.

IPsec IKE / IKE with NAT traversal
DNS over TLS / HTTP/3 over QUIC

theoryAdd.plainText: Sliding-window utilisation U = min(1, W/(1 + 2a)); a window of 1 + 2a frames keeps the link busy (a = t_prop / t_frame)

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1: window-limited TCP
Given R = 100 Mbps, fibre 1,500 km at 2 x 10^8 m/s, window W = 65,535 bytes
t_prop = 1.5 x 10^6 m / (2 x 10^8 m/s) = 7.5 ms, so RTT = 15 ms
W / RTT = 65,535 x 8 bits / 0.015 s = 34.95 Mbps
Throughput = min(100, 34.95) = 34.95 Mbps: the window, not the link, is the limit
Window to fill the pipe = R x RTT = 10^8 x 0.015 = 1.5 x 10^6 bits = 187,500 bytes
Window scale shift 1: 65,535 x 2 = 131,070 < 187,500 (too small)
Window scale shift 2: 65,535 x 4 = 262,140 >= 187,500, so shift 2 is the minimum

Worked example 2: from channel capacity to window size
Channel B = 500 kHz, S/N = 255 (about 24 dB); frames of 1,000 bytes; t_prop = 5 ms
Shannon: C = 500 x 10^3 x log2(1 + 255) = 500 x 10^3 x 8 = 4 Mbps
t_frame = 8,000 bits / 4 Mbps = 2 ms, so a = 5 / 2 = 2.5
Stop-and-wait: U = 1 / (1 + 2a) = 1/6 = 16.7 %, about 0.667 Mbps of the 4 Mbps
Frames needed in flight to keep the link busy: 1 + 2a = 6
Go-Back-N: 2^m - 1 >= 6 gives m = 3 bits (window 7)
Selective repeat: 2^(m-1) >= 6 gives m = 4 bits (window 8)

Worked trace: loading http://www.example.com/ with empty ARP and DNS caches
PC 10.0.0.25/24, default gateway 10.0.0.1, DNS server 8.8.8.8
1  ARP   who-has 10.0.0.1? sent to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff; reply: 10.0.0.1 is-at <router MAC>
2  DNS   query A www.example.com, UDP 10.0.0.25:53001 -> 8.8.8.8:53 (frame to router MAC)
3  DNS   answer A 93.184.216.34
4  TCP   SYN      10.0.0.25:50123 -> 93.184.216.34:80
5  TCP   SYN-ACK  93.184.216.34:80 -> 10.0.0.25:50123
6  TCP   ACK, then HTTP GET / HTTP/1.1 with Host: www.example.com
7  HTTP  200 OK carries the page; the connection stays open (persistent by default)
Only one ARP: 8.8.8.8 and 93.184.216.34 are off-link, so every frame goes to the router's MAC

Slips to watch for across this chapter: putting a dB value straight into Shannon's formula; mixing one-way delay and round-trip time (a = t_prop/t_frame is one-way, while the CSMA/CD minimum frame and window/RTT use the round trip); forgetting the −2 in 2^h − 2; mixing bits and bytes when a window in bytes meets a rate in bits per second; using the Go-Back-N window 2^m − 1 for Selective Repeat, which allows only 2^(m−1); ARPing for a remote host instead of the default gateway; and choosing SSL or WEP where TLS or WPA2/WPA3 is the current answer.

questions.questionText: Which row correctly describes TCP and UDP?
options: TCP: connectionless, best-effort, 8-byte header; UDP: connection-oriented, reliable, 20–60-byte header
TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, 20–60-byte header; UDP: connectionless, best-effort, 8-byte header
TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, 8-byte header; UDP: connectionless, best-effort, 20–60-byte header
TCP: connection-oriented, best-effort, 20–60-byte header; UDP: connectionless, reliable, 8-byte header
questions.explanation: TCP sets up a connection with a three-way handshake and makes delivery reliable with sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission; its header is 20 bytes without options and up to 60 with them. UDP sends independent datagrams with an 8-byte header and no delivery guarantee.

questions.questionText: Match each device with the OSI layer it works at and the unit of data it handles: hub, switch and router.
options: Hub: layer 1, bits; switch: layer 2, frames; router: layer 3, packets
Hub: layer 2, frames; switch: layer 3, packets; router: layer 4, segments
Hub: layer 1, bits; switch: layer 1, bits; router: layer 2, frames
Hub: layer 3, packets; switch: layer 2, frames; router: layer 1, bits
questions.explanation: A hub only regenerates and repeats bits (physical layer), a switch forwards frames by MAC address (data link layer), and a router forwards packets by IP address (network layer).

questions.questionText: Alice sends a message from her desktop mail client to bob@b.com. Bob reads his mail on both his phone and his laptop and wants it kept in folders on the server. Which sequence of protocols carries the message from Alice to Bob's screen?
options: POP3 from Alice's client to her server (port 110), a DNS A lookup for b.com, SMTP relay (port 25), then IMAP to read it
SMTP submission (port 587), a DNS MX lookup for b.com, SMTP relay (port 25), then POP3 (port 110), which downloads each message to one device and deletes it from the server
HTTP upload to Alice's server (port 80), FTP transfer between the mail servers (port 21), then SMTP (port 25) to deliver it to Bob's devices
SMTP submission to Alice's server (port 587), a DNS MX lookup for b.com, SMTP relay to b.com's mail server (port 25), then IMAP (143, or 993 with TLS) to read it
questions.explanation: The client submits the message by SMTP on port 587; Alice's server looks up the MX record of b.com and relays the message by SMTP to port 25; Bob's devices then read it with IMAP, which keeps mail and folders on the server. POP3 only retrieves mail, normally downloading it to a single device.

questions.questionText: Which of these is NOT a routing algorithm?
options: Distance vector (Bellman–Ford)
Link state (Dijkstra's shortest path)
Selective repeat
Flooding
questions.explanation: Distance vector, link state (which runs Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm) and flooding all decide the paths that packets take through a network. Selective repeat is an ARQ method for retransmitting lost frames or segments, a job of the data link and transport layers.

questions.questionText: Which option correctly matches IEEE 802.3, 802.4, 802.5 and 802.11 with their LAN types and medium access methods?
options: 802.3 Ethernet, CSMA/CA; 802.4 token ring, a token passed round a ring; 802.5 token bus, a token passed round a logical ring on a bus; 802.11 Wi-Fi, CSMA/CD
802.3 Ethernet, CSMA/CD; 802.4 token bus, a token passed round a logical ring on a bus; 802.5 token ring, a token passed round a ring; 802.11 Wi-Fi, CSMA/CA
802.3 Ethernet, CSMA/CD; 802.4 token ring, a token passed round a ring; 802.5 token bus, a token passed round a logical ring on a bus; 802.11 Wi-Fi, CSMA/CA
802.3 Ethernet, CSMA/CD; 802.4 token bus, a token passed round a logical ring on a bus; 802.5 token ring, a token passed round a ring; 802.11 Wi-Fi, CSMA/CD
questions.explanation: 802.3 Ethernet senses the carrier and detects collisions (CSMA/CD); 802.4 token bus and 802.5 token ring avoid collisions by passing a token; 802.11 Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA because a radio cannot detect a collision while it is sending.

questions.questionText: Which command shows the sequence of routers that packets pass through on their way to a destination?
options: ping
ipconfig
netstat
traceroute (tracert on Windows)
questions.explanation: traceroute sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3 and so on, and each router that drops a probe returns ICMP Time Exceeded, revealing itself. ping only tests reachability and round-trip time, ipconfig shows the local interface settings, and netstat lists connections and listening ports.

questions.questionText: A user cannot open www.example.com by name, but the same website opens when she types its IP address into the browser. Which service is most likely failing?
options: DNS name resolution
The web server's HTTP service
TCP on the user's PC
The default gateway (router)
questions.explanation: Reaching the site by its IP address proves that routing, TCP and the web server all work; only the translation of the name into an address fails. The next step is to check the DNS server configured on the PC (queries go to port 53).

questions.questionText: A small office divides its class C network 192.168.10.0/24 into 4 equal subnets (subnet zero is used). What is the subnet mask, how many usable hosts does each subnet have, and what is the broadcast address of the third subnet?
questions.explanation: Four subnets need 2 borrowed bits (2^2 = 4), giving /26 = 255.255.255.192 with 6 host bits and 2^6 − 2 = 62 usable hosts. The subnets start at .0, .64, .128 and .192, so the third is 192.168.10.128/26, whose broadcast address is 192.168.10.191.

questions.questionText: To make sure that an attacker cannot change a message in transit without the receiver noticing, what should be sent with the message?
options: Nothing extra: encryption without any integrity check is enough
A message authentication code (a keyed hash such as HMAC) or a digital signature
A CRC-32 or an unkeyed hash, such as SHA-256, of the message
A compressed copy of the message
questions.explanation: An attacker who changes the message can simply recompute a CRC or an unkeyed hash, and encryption without an integrity check does not reveal tampering. A MAC needs the shared secret key and a signature needs the sender's private key, so a modified message fails verification.

questions.questionText: RIP is a distance vector protocol and OSPF a link state protocol. How are RIP, OSPF and BGP messages carried, respectively?
options: RIP over TCP port 520; OSPF in UDP to port 89; BGP in UDP to port 179
RIP in UDP to port 520; OSPF over TCP port 89; BGP over TCP port 179
RIP directly in IP as protocol 89; OSPF in UDP to port 520; BGP over TCP port 179
RIP in UDP to port 520; OSPF directly in IP as protocol 89; BGP over TCP port 179
questions.explanation: RIP messages are UDP datagrams to port 520, OSPF packets go straight into IP with protocol number 89 and use no transport protocol, and BGP peers talk over a TCP connection to port 179. BGP is the path vector protocol used between autonomous systems.

questions.questionText: Which statement about TCP, IPv6, HTTPS and hubs is TRUE?
options: TCP is faster than UDP because TCP has the smaller header
IPv6 addresses are 32 bits long
HTTPS protects HTTP with TLS, the successor of the now-deprecated SSL
A hub operates at layer 3
questions.explanation: HTTPS is HTTP carried inside a TLS connection, by default on TCP port 443; SSL itself is deprecated. TCP's header is at least 20 bytes against UDP's 8, IPv6 addresses are 128 bits and a hub works at layer 1.

questions.questionText: Which statement about Wi-Fi security, TCP, DNS and routers is NOT correct?
options: WEP is secure enough for a new Wi-Fi network as long as its longest (128-bit) key option is chosen
TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake
DNS uses port 53, over UDP for ordinary queries and over TCP for zone transfers
A router operates at layer 3 and forwards packets by IP address
questions.explanation: Flaws in the way WEP uses RC4 with a short 24-bit IV let an attacker recover the key in minutes, whatever the key length, so new networks must use WPA2 (AES-CCMP) or WPA3. The other three statements are correct.

questions.questionText: The memory aid 'A T I N' lists the four TCP/IP layers from the top: Application, Transport, Internet and Network access. Which list gives a correct example protocol for each layer, in that order?
options: TCP, HTTP, Ethernet, IP
DNS, IP, TCP, PPP
SMTP, TCP, Ethernet, IP
HTTP, UDP, ICMP, Ethernet
questions.explanation: HTTP is an application protocol, UDP a transport protocol, ICMP travels inside IP at the internet layer, and Ethernet belongs to the network access (link) layer. The other lists put IP, TCP or Ethernet in the wrong layer.

questions.questionText: A TCP connection is identified by its 4-tuple: source IP address, source port, destination IP address and destination port. How many bits does the 4-tuple contain over IPv4, and over IPv6?
options: 64 bits over IPv4, 256 bits over IPv6
96 bits over IPv4, 288 bits over IPv6
48 bits over IPv4, 144 bits over IPv6
128 bits over IPv4, 320 bits over IPv6
questions.explanation: Addresses are 32 bits in IPv4 and 128 bits in IPv6, and each port is 16 bits: 32 + 32 + 16 + 16 = 96 bits and 128 + 128 + 16 + 16 = 288 bits. Leaving out the ports gives 64 and 256, and counting one endpoint only gives 48 and 144.

questions.questionText: A DHCP server leases addresses on the subnet 10.20.30.0/23. The router's interface uses 10.20.30.1, and 10 printers have static addresses from the same subnet, which are excluded from the pool. How many addresses can the pool lease to clients?
questions.explanation: A /23 leaves 32 − 23 = 9 host bits: 2^9 − 2 = 510 usable addresses, from 10.20.30.1 to 10.20.31.254. Taking away the router's address and the 10 printers leaves 510 − 11 = 499. 500 forgets the router, 501 forgets the network and broadcast addresses, and 243 treats the subnet as a /24.

questions.questionText: Linux ping sends 56 data bytes by default and reports '64 bytes from 10.0.0.1'. What is the IPv4 Total Length of each Echo Request (no IP options), and how long is the Ethernet II frame that carries it, counting the Ethernet header and FCS but not the preamble?
options: Total Length 84 bytes; frame 102 bytes
Total Length 64 bytes; frame 82 bytes
Total Length 76 bytes; frame 94 bytes
Total Length 84 bytes; frame 98 bytes
questions.explanation: The ICMP message is an 8-byte header plus 56 data bytes = 64 bytes, the figure ping reports. IPv4 adds 20 bytes (Total Length 84), and Ethernet adds a 14-byte header and a 4-byte FCS: 84 + 18 = 102 bytes, above the 64-byte minimum, so no padding is needed.

questions.questionText: N stations share a 48 kbps pure ALOHA channel (1 kbps = 1000 bit/s). Each station sends a 1,000-bit frame on average once every 50 s, and a station keeps any frame it cannot yet send in a buffer. What is the largest N the channel can support?
options: About 883
About 441
questions.explanation: The channel has 48,000 / 1,000 = 48 frame times per second, and pure ALOHA delivers at most 18.4 % of them: 0.184 × 48 ≈ 8.83 frames/s. Each station needs 1/50 = 0.02 frames/s, so N ≤ 8.83 / 0.02 ≈ 441; 883 uses the slotted ALOHA maximum (36.8 %), and 1,200 and 2,400 assume 50 % and 100 % throughput.

questions.questionText: Which statement about ARP, switches, routers and ICMP is NOT correct?
options: ARP requests are link-layer broadcasts, so routers do not forward them
A switch fills its MAC address table by sending ARP requests for every host on the LAN
An IPv4 router decrements the TTL and recomputes the header checksum of every packet it forwards
ICMP messages are carried inside IP datagrams, so they are routed like any other packet
questions.explanation: A switch learns passively: it records the source MAC address of each arriving frame against the port it came in on, and it does not use ARP for this. The other three statements are correct.

questions.questionText: A faulty memory chip in a router flips one bit in the TCP payload of an IPv4 packet after the incoming frame's FCS has already been checked. The router forwards the packet in a new Ethernet frame with a freshly computed FCS. Which check detects the error?
options: The FCS check at the next hop, because CRC-32 covers the whole frame
The IPv4 header checksum at the next router
The TCP checksum at the destination host
None; the corrupted data is certain to reach the application
questions.explanation: The new FCS is computed over the already-corrupted packet, so the next CRC check passes, and the IPv4 checksum covers only the header. The TCP checksum is checked end to end over a pseudo-header, the TCP header and the data, so the destination catches the flipped bit and discards the segment, which the sender then retransmits.

questions.questionText: Which pairing of an attack with the protocol weakness it exploits is NOT correct?
options: ARP spoofing: forged ARP replies, which an attacker can send to a victim from anywhere on the Internet
SYN flood: the server keeps state for every half-open TCP connection
DNS cache poisoning: a resolver accepts a forged UDP reply that matches its query's ID and port
Smurf attack: ICMP Echo Requests sent to a directed broadcast address with the victim's address as the source
questions.explanation: ARP is not routed: its requests and replies stay on one link, so an ARP spoofer must be on the victim's LAN or control a host there. The other three pairings are correct.

questions.questionText: Which entry on a networking formula sheet is NOT correct?
options: Pure ALOHA: S = G·e^(−2G), with a maximum of 18.4 % at G = 0.5
Slotted ALOHA: S = G·e^(−G), with a maximum of 36.8 % at G = 1
CSMA/CD minimum frame length = one-way propagation delay × bit rate
Stop-and-wait utilisation = 1/(1 + 2a), where a = t_prop / t_frame
questions.explanation: A sender must still be transmitting when a collision from the far end gets back to it, so the frame must last a full round trip: L_min = 2 × t_prop × R. The one-way version gives only half the minimum; the other three entries are correct.

questions.questionText: A firewall must allow a LAN's hosts to use DNS (ordinary queries), DHCP, HTTPS (HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, not HTTP/3) and SSH. Which set of rules opens the correct transport protocols and ports?
options: TCP 53; TCP 67 and 68; TCP 443; UDP 22
UDP 53; UDP 67 and 68; UDP 443; TCP 23
UDP 53; TCP 67 and 68; TCP 443; TCP 22
UDP 53; UDP 67 and 68; TCP 443; TCP 22
questions.explanation: Ordinary DNS queries use UDP 53, DHCP uses UDP 67 (server) and 68 (client), HTTPS over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 runs on TCP 443, and SSH on TCP 22. TCP 23 is Telnet, and only HTTP/3 over QUIC would need UDP 443.

questions.questionText: PC 192.168.1.20/24 has default gateway 192.168.1.1 and DNS server 192.168.1.53, and its ARP and DNS caches are empty. The user opens http://www.example.com/, whose server is 93.184.216.34. Using IPv4 only, in which order does the PC send these messages?
options: ARP request for 192.168.1.1, DNS query, TCP SYN to port 80, HTTP GET
ARP request for 192.168.1.53, DNS query, ARP request for 192.168.1.1, TCP SYN to port 80, HTTP GET
DNS query, ARP request for 93.184.216.34, TCP SYN to port 80, HTTP GET
ARP request for 192.168.1.53, DNS query, ARP request for 93.184.216.34, TCP SYN to port 80, HTTP GET
questions.explanation: The DNS server is on the PC's own /24, so the PC ARPs for it directly before sending the query. The web server is off-link, so the PC then ARPs for its default gateway (never for the remote address), opens TCP with a SYN to port 80 and sends the GET once the handshake is complete.

questions.questionText: A VoIP call sends 50 packets per second in each direction. Each packet carries 160 bytes of voice behind a 12-byte RTP header, over UDP and IPv6 (no extension headers) in Ethernet II frames. Counting the Ethernet header and FCS but not the preamble or inter-frame gap, what fraction of each frame is voice, and what bit rate does one direction use (1 kbps = 1000 bit/s)?
questions.explanation: Frame = 160 + 12 (RTP) + 8 (UDP) + 40 (IPv6) + 18 (Ethernet header and FCS) = 238 bytes, so voice is 160/238 = 67.2 %. Rate = 238 × 8 × 50 = 95,200 bit/s = 95.2 kbps; 87.2 kbps uses a 20-byte IPv4 header, 88.0 kbps leaves out Ethernet, and 11.9 is the rate in kilobytes per second.

questions.questionText: A 10 MB file (1 MB = 10^6 bytes) is sent over TCP with a fixed window of 125,000 bytes on a 1 Gbps link across a 2,000 km fibre path (signal speed 2 × 10^8 m/s). Using throughput ≈ min(link rate, window/RTT) and ignoring the handshake, slow start, headers and processing, about how long does the transfer take?
questions.explanation: The one-way delay is 2 × 10^6 m ÷ (2 × 10^8 m/s) = 10 ms, so RTT = 20 ms and the window allows 125,000 × 8 bits ÷ 0.02 s = 50 Mbps, well below 1 Gbps. The file is 8 × 10^7 bits, so it takes about 8 × 10^7 ÷ (5 × 10^7 bit/s) = 1.6 s; 0.8 s uses the one-way delay as the RTT, 0.08 s ignores the window and 12.8 s treats the window as bits.

questions.questionText: A channel with a bandwidth of 3 MHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 15 is run at its Shannon capacity. Stop-and-wait sends 1,500-byte frames over it with a one-way propagation delay of 1.5 ms; ACK transmission and processing times are ignored. What is the effective throughput?
options: 12 Mbps
4.8 Mbps
1.71 Mbps
3 Mbps
questions.explanation: C = 3 MHz × log₂(1 + 15) = 12 Mbps, so t_frame = 12,000 bits ÷ 12 Mbps = 1 ms and a = 1.5 ms ÷ 1 ms = 1.5. U = 1/(1 + 2a) = 1/4, giving 0.25 × 12 = 3 Mbps; 4.8 Mbps comes from 1/(1 + a), and 1.71 Mbps from using the round trip as t_prop.

questions.questionText: A 10 Mbps link (1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s) has a one-way propagation delay of 10 ms. It carries 1,250-byte frames, each containing 50 bytes of header and trailer, using Go-Back-N with 4-bit sequence numbers and the largest window allowed. Ignoring errors, ACK transmission and processing times, what is the throughput of user data?
options: About 6.86 Mbps
About 7.14 Mbps
About 3.66 Mbps
9.6 Mbps
questions.explanation: t_frame = 10,000 bits ÷ 10 Mbps = 1 ms, so a = 10 and 1 + 2a = 21 frames would fill the pipe. The window is 2^4 − 1 = 15, so U = 15/21 = 71.4 %, and only 1,200 of every 1,250 bytes are user data: 10 × 0.714 × 0.96 ≈ 6.86 Mbps (7.14 ignores the header, 3.66 uses the Selective Repeat window of 8, and 9.6 assumes the window fills the pipe).

questions.questionText: Host A is 172.20.37.200/21 with default gateway 172.20.32.1, and its ARP cache is empty. It sends one packet to host B at 172.20.39.250 and one to host C at 172.20.40.9. For which IP address does A send an ARP request in each case?
options: For B it asks for 172.20.32.1; for C it asks for 172.20.40.9
For B it asks for 172.20.39.250; for C it asks for 172.20.32.1
In both cases it asks for the destination's own address
In both cases it asks for 172.20.32.1
questions.explanation: A /21 covers 8 values of the third octet, so A's subnet runs from 172.20.32.0 to 172.20.39.255. B lies inside it and is reached directly, so A ARPs for B; C lies outside, so A ARPs for its gateway and hands the frame to the router. Assuming a /16 or a /24 gives the last two answers.

questions.questionText: A routing loop makes R1 send packets for network N to R2, and R2 send them straight back to R1. A host on R1's LAN sends a packet for N with TTL = 64, and every router decrements TTL by 1. How many times does the packet cross the R1–R2 link, and what does the source receive?
options: 64 times; ICMP Time Exceeded (type 11) from R1
63 times; ICMP Destination Unreachable (type 3) from R2
63 times; ICMP Time Exceeded (type 11) from R2
It keeps circulating until the routing protocol removes the loop, and no ICMP message is sent
questions.explanation: R1 receives the packet with TTL 64, R2 with 63, R1 with 62 and so on; the router that receives TTL 1 decrements it to 0 and drops the packet. That is the 64th router visit, an even-numbered one and so R2, after 63 crossings of the link, and R2 returns ICMP Time Exceeded (type 11, code 0) to the source.
